title: AI helped me build a pipe puzzle. Now someone needs to knock me off the leaderboard.
author: Right-Mess-6418
selftext:
I'm building Luma Loop with Codex, using React/TypeScript and Firebase. It's a free browser puzzle: rotate pipes, connect every star, and bring the light home.



The useful lesson so far has been how much player feedback changes the work you ask AI to do. One player called out the generic colours, small type and wordy UI. Another problem was difficulty: increasing the grid size didn't necessarily create a better puzzle.



The latest release replaces the first five personal loops with authored layouts built around route choices, star branches and linked pipes. Codex helped implement those layouts and their known-solution checks. Older saved boards and serialized friend challenges keep their existing layouts, so changing the opening doesn't rewrite someone's ongoing puzzle.



The design change I care about is giving players something to notice: reaching home can look correct while leaving a star disconnected. The UI now makes that objective explicit. There is also an optional harder-puzzle preview without losing your saved loop.



If you use AI for puzzle design, how do you check that harder means more deduction rather than just more clicking?



And a small challenge for anyone who wants to play: reach Loop 53. My benchmark is 52 completed loops and 93,161 points as CircuitFox. Apparently building the game has done terrible things to my confidence.



[https://luma-loop.web.app/](https://luma-loop.web.app/)



Guest play is available; an account is needed to appear on the public leaderboard. I'm the creator, and development is AI-assisted.
